verses.note: Before Israel has a tabernacle, priesthood, or law code, God gives it a calendar. Worship begins with the ordering of time around what God has done, so that the year itself becomes a confession of redemption.

Worship is described with the same word as slavery, but the master has changed. The exodus is not freedom from all service but release into the service of the God who frees, which is why the ritual of remembrance is itself called avodah.
Worship is placed where God chooses to make his name known, and its goal is his coming to bless. The altar is not a way to summon God but a place where he promises to meet his people.
The feasts gather harvest and history into one act of worship. Israel's thanksgiving for grain is also a remembrance of rescue, so that the rhythm of the farming year keeps the exodus in view.

The renewed covenant ends with the ordinary details of offering: the right bread, the right timing, the best of the harvest. Faithfulness to God is expressed in small acts of worship repeated every year.

The day ends not with the removal of sin but with burnt offerings, the gift of the whole animal to God. Cleansing opens the way to renewed worship, and the priest returns to his ordinary service in his ordinary robes.

The remedy for private, unregulated sacrifice is not to forbid eating meat but to bring it to God's house as a peace offering. Worship is gathered to the place and the mediation God appoints, and the meal itself becomes fellowship with him.
Fear, service, and oath cover the inward stance, the outward practice, and the public commitment of worship. All three are reserved for the LORD.

The phrase that describes the Levites' status becomes, in the Psalms, a prayer any believer can make. Psalm 16:5 and 73:26 call the LORD the speaker's portion, taking the Levites' privilege as a picture of what God is to every faithful person.
God is enjoyed as a possession, not only obeyed as a master. The Levites' status becomes a model for every believer, as in Psalm 73:26 and Lamentations 3:24.
God's throne among his people is their praise. The sufferer, who cannot now praise, remembers where God is found, and the psalm will end with him restored to that praise (verses 22-25).

No offering is adequate to God, not even the whole of Lebanon on the altar. Worship cannot enlarge him; it can only acknowledge him, which is the point of Psalm 50:9-12 and of Paul's words in Athens that God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25).
Restoration is not complete when people are back on their land; it is complete when they are gathered before God together. The first thing the reunited people do is go up to worship.

The Magi's purpose is worship from their first sentence. Proskyneō can mean homage to a king, but Matthew uses it for what is owed to God alone (4:10) and for the disciples' worship of the risen Jesus (28:9, 17), so the Gospel's first worshipers already point to its last.

Herod uses the language of worship to cover murder. The Gospel's first counterfeit worshiper is a king, and Jesus will later quote Isaiah against people who honor God with their lips while their hearts are far from him (15:8).

Joy comes before the worship of verse 11 and is part of it. Matthew's intensified language presents the Magi's gladness as the fitting response to finding the Messiah, a joy the Gospel will not describe this fully again until the resurrection.

The Magi's worship has three movements that Matthew's verbs mark: they come, they fall down, they give. Worship in the Gospel's first scene of it is bodily and costly, directed to a child who has done nothing yet but be who he is.

Worship and service belong to God alone, and the two verbs cannot be divided: to bow is to serve. Jesus refuses proskynēsis to any creature, yet in Matthew he receives it from the Magi, the disciples in the boat, and the women and the Eleven after the resurrection (2:11, 14:33, 28:9, 28:17), a silent claim about who he is.

Worship offered while a brother's grievance is ignored is out of order. Jesus stands in the prophets' tradition that God does not want sacrifice without justice and mercy (Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21-24), which Matthew quotes twice (9:13; 12:7).
The verse locates the value of devotion in the one it is offered to. The same act of prayer or giving can be worship of God or a bid for human praise, and the difference is invisible from outside.

Fasting is presented as a normal part of devotion to God (‘when you fast’), not an optional extra; Jesus later says his disciples will fast when the bridegroom is taken away (9:15). Its value lies in being directed to the Father.

Jesus does not abolish fasting; he times it. His disciples will fast ‘then’, and the early church did (Acts 13:2-3, 14:23). Christian fasting is shaped by the bridegroom's absence and the longing for his return, not by merit.

Hosea's words, as Jesus uses them, do not abolish sacrifice or ritual but set them beneath mercy. Worship that is scrupulous about observance and careless about people has inverted God's order of priorities.

In a Gospel where Jesus himself quotes the command to worship God alone (4:10), the disciples worship Jesus and he accepts it. This is the first time in Matthew that the disciples do so; the Magi did it at his birth (2:11), and the women and the Eleven will do it after the resurrection (28:9, 17).

Worship is measured by the heart, not the lips, and worship built on human rules taught as God's is empty. The prophets said the same of sacrifice without obedience (Hosea 6:6, which Matthew quotes in 9:13 and 12:7). The verse warns every tradition that performs devotion while the heart is elsewhere.

Worship that pleases God is first love for him and for neighbor; ritual without it is empty. The scribe's words, spoken in sight of the altar, prepare for the temple's end in chapter 13 and for a worship no longer bound to sacrifice.

The widow's offering is the chapter's last picture of true worship: given wholly to God, unseen by the crowd, and seen by Jesus. Jesus himself is about to give his whole life, as the passion narrative will show.

The soldiers kneel to Jesus in contempt, and Mark records it with the verb for worship. Philippians 2:10 foresees every knee bowing to Jesus in truth; the mockery of the praetorium is the upside-down version of that scene.

By the time of Paul and Luke, Christians gathered and collected gifts on ‘the first day of the week’ (1 Corinthians 16:2, Acts 20:7), and John calls it ‘the Lord's day’ (Revelation 1:10). The verse is where that practice begins: Christian worship moved to Sunday because of what the women found on it.
Restored speech is used first for blessing God. Luke's narrative repeatedly ends healing and deliverance in praise (5:25, 13:13, 17:15, 18:43).
Deliverance has a purpose beyond safety: worship without fear. The exodus pattern holds: God frees his people so they may serve him.
Heaven's first response to the birth is praise. The song orders worship rightly: God's glory first, then peace as his gift.
Earth echoes heaven. The shepherds return to the same work in the same fields, and what has changed is that they praise.
Jesus is raised within Israel's yearly rhythm of worship. His later Passover in Jerusalem (22:7-20) will give the feast its fulfillment.
Worship belongs to God alone. Jesus, who later receives worship after the resurrection (24:52), here refuses to give it to any creature, and his answer defines worship as undivided service.
The healed man and the crowd give glory to God, not merely to Jesus. Luke presents Jesus' works as acts of God that rightly end in praise of God.

Mary's portion is to sit before the Lord and receive his word, the posture of worship. The psalmists' confession that the Lord is their portion (Psalm 16:5, 73:26) stands behind the promise that this portion will not be taken away.

Worship in this verse is gratitude that turns back to its source. The man praises God and thanks Jesus with the same act of return, which Jesus in verse 18 calls giving glory to God. Luke lets the reader see that thanksgiving directed to Jesus is received as glory to God.

Healing issues in following and in praise, both from the man and from the crowd. Luke closes the scene the way he closes many of Jesus' works, with God glorified (5:25-26, 7:16, 13:13), so that every healing becomes an occasion of worship directed to God.

The disciples' praise is directed to God for what he has done through Jesus. Luke's Gospel is framed by such praise, from the angels and shepherds at the birth (2:13, 2:20) to the disciples blessing God in the temple at the end (24:53).

Luke has taken care to show that worship belongs to God alone (4:8). When the disciples now worship Jesus, and Luke records it without correction, the Gospel's last scene confesses what the creeds later state: the risen Son shares the honor due to God.

The question assumes that true worship depends on the right place. It was a serious and biblical question, since Deuteronomy tied sacrifice to the place God would choose, and Jesus does not mock it. He answers by showing that the place is being redefined by the hour that has come.

True worship is defined by its object (the Father), its medium (spirit), and its content (truth), not its location. And it begins with the Father's search: God seeks worshipers before worshipers seek God, the same movement as the shepherd seeking the lost (Luke 15:4) and the Son who came to seek and save (Luke 19:10).

Jesus keeps Israel's festivals. The conflict of this chapter is not between Jesus and Israel's worship but between Jesus and a reading of the Sabbath that could not see God at work in the healing he did on it.

Israel's God will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). Yet here all are to honor the Son as they honor the Father. The verse is one of the clearest grounds for the early Christian practice of worshiping Jesus, which the church understood not as a second worship but as the one worship of the one God.

The man expelled from the synagogue's worship worships Jesus, with the verb the Gospel reserved for the Father in chapter 4. John offers no correction, as angels and apostles offer when others bow to them (Acts 10:25-26, Revelation 19:10), which is one of the ways the Gospel shows Jesus sharing the Father's honor (5:23).
The first believers kept worshiping at the temple and ate together at home. Their praise of God is joyful and daily, tied to ordinary meals as well as to the temple's hours of prayer.
Trust is itself worship. To believe that God is able to do what he promised is to give him the glory the rest of humanity withheld.
The end of reconciliation is joy in God himself, not only in his gifts. The boast that was excluded in 3:27 is restored, redirected from self to God.
Paul's teaching on the resurrection ends in thanks, not speculation. The proper response to doctrine is praise to the God who gives what we could never achieve.

The letter's theology begins as praise. Election, redemption, and the gift of the Spirit are first of all reasons to bless God, and the refrain ‘to the praise of His glory’ (verses 6, 12, 14) keeps the whole sentence pointed toward worship.
What the temple barrier prevented, Gentiles approaching God, is now open to both groups equally. Worship is defined by access through Christ, not by a place or an ethnic boundary.
Angels are commanded to worship the Son. Since Scripture reserves worship for God alone, and Revelation 22:8-9 has an angel refusing it, the verse places the Son on the side of God.
The risen Jesus leads his people's praise. Christian worship is pictured as the Son singing to the Father in the midst of his brothers and sisters, not merely as people singing about him.

What was once restricted to the high priest once a year (Leviticus 16:2) is now the ordinary privilege of God's people. The verse reshapes worship around access through Christ rather than through a sanctuary on earth.
The first covenant's worship was God-given, regulated in detail. Hebrews does not treat it as human invention to be despised but as a divinely ordered pattern whose meaning is now disclosed.
The goal of cleansing is service: ‘to serve the living God’. Forgiveness is not an end in itself but admission to the priestly worship that Israel's priests alone once offered.
The second beast is religion put in the service of power. It does not demand worship for itself but for the first beast, which is what makes it dangerous: counterfeit worship can look like a lamb.
